newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe threatens to defy ban on trade in ivory.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe threatens to defy ban on trade in ivory.

text.p: Zimbabwe served notice on Monday that it would defy a world ban on ivory trade if it failed to win an exemption at a forum in Harare on endangered species.
It accused some opponents of the trade in ivory of racism.
Environment and Tourism Minister Chen Chimutengwende said Zimbabwe would not accept a compromise at the 10-day Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) ending on Friday.
Environmental pressure groups campaigning against reopening the ivory trade said Zimbabwe's threat would not influence their position.
Zimbabwe, Botswana and Namibia have asked CITES for an exemption from the 1989 ban on ivory trade on grounds that their combined 150,000-elephant herd is excessive and not endangered.
They are backed by Japan but face fierce opposition from many Western powers, including the United States and France, which say reopening trade would put elephants at risk worldwide.
"Zimbabwe will go it alone and sell ivory without CITES approval rather than accept a compromise," Chimutengwende was quoted as saying in an interview with the state-controlled Herald newspaper.

But Chimutengwende told a briefing later on Monday that Zimbabwe was still confident of winning the support of two-thirds of the 138-member CITES later this week to resume trade, initially in the 40-tonne stock it has accumulated since the ban.

"I don't want to concentrate on what we will do if we lose because I am confident we are going to win. If we lose out, we will cross the bridge when we come to it," he said to persistent queries on who Zimbabwe would trade with.
Zimbabwe entered a reservation when the ivory sales embargo was imposed which means it could trade if it wanted to, but only if it found willing trading partners in or outside the CITES.
"There are a number of countries we can do business with, but we are not talking about that now," Chimutengwende said.
Delegates from Namibia, Botswana and Japan -- which wants to buy the ivory from southern Africa -- refused to spell out what they would do if they lost the vote this week.
"We are assuming we are winning," said one Japanese official who declined to be named.
Pat Awori, a spokeswoman for Special Survival Network (SNN), a grouping of over 40 international non-governmental environmental watchdogs, said she regretted Zimbabwe's new position.
"But it does not change our own position. We remain opposed to any resumption in ivory trade because of the knock-on effects it may have around the world," she said on the fringes of the forum.

"That (Zimbabwe's unilateral decision to resume) will be unfortunate because it will affect future cooperation and dialogue not just on this issue but other problems of Africa...and there are many," said Awori, who is based in Kenya.

Chimutengwende told the Herald Zimbabwe would not accept a compromise being suggested by some delegates to downlist the African elephant to species meant for controlled trade, with no trading quotas immediately allocated from the "no trade list".

"This will be totally unacceptable to us and CITES will have made itself irrelevant to us because instead of rewarding us, it will be punishing us for successful conservation policies which have resulted in our having so many animals, including the elephants," he said, adding:

"There are others who are just racist and do not like urbanisation or development of Africa because they like Africa to be one big zoo where they will just come as tourists and see poor blacks practising their traditions and living with wild animals".
Awori rejected the racism charges, saying: "They just don't stick."
